claims.text: Post-synthesis thermal annealing reduces Cu surface segregation in Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
Reducing Cu surface segregation homogenizes the nanoparticles' surface chemistry.
Surface homogenization increases the activation energy for premelting.
Surface homogenization makes the melting transition more abrupt.
The as-synthesized Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles are produced by inert-gas condensation.
As-synthesized Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles exhibit surface chemical inhomogeneity.
The initial surface chemical inhomogeneity is caused by preferential Cu segregation.
Cu is the lower-melting component of the Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticle system.
Cu has lower cohesive energy than the other relevant components.
Cu's lower cohesive energy causes it to segregate to the nanoparticle surface during synthesis.
Cu surface segregation creates a chemically distinct outer shell.
The chemically distinct Cu-rich outer shell lowers the premelting barrier.
Controlled thermal annealing facilitates elemental interdiffusion and surface homogenization.
Surface homogenization increases surface cohesive energy.
Increasing surface cohesive energy raises the energy barrier for the onset of premelting.
Annealed nanoparticles will have a higher premelting onset temperature than as-synthesized nanoparticles.
Annealed nanoparticles will have a sharper melting transition than as-synthesized nanoparticles.
The hypothesis is limited to conditions where annealing reduces surface segregation without significant coarsening or phase separation.
The hypothesis may not apply under extreme annealing conditions or when synthesis does not produce initial surface segregation.
Unintended particle coarsening during annealing may alter the premelting onset and melting-transition abruptness.
